title: Shape-based Figure-Ground Organization in Vision Transformers
claim: Linear probes on frozen encoders trained on natural images transfer zero-shot to cue-controlled stimuli, so the learned signal relies on shape rather than texture.
layout: 3 panels: pipeline and stimuli left, scatter plot right, with legend
description: The left two-thirds show the experimental protocol. The first column, 'Train probes on natural images', shows a mushroom photo and its figure-ground mask, with black border patches excluded. A frozen ViT block (embedding, then repeated Attn+FFN layers) feeds a row of probe boxes, with arrows from each layer down to a probe. Below it, 'Evaluate on natural images' shows a hot-air balloon and an egret photo. The middle column, 'Evaluate zero-shot generalization', shows balloon stimuli with swapped textures (dark blue noise, silk, checker) beside their flat-color masks. The right panel is a scatter plot of texturized accuracy against natural accuracy, with a diagonal line. Points are colored by training objective and marked filled or open for pretrained or random init. Black baseline markers for spatial prior, area, center overlap and offset are included. Most models cluster near the diagonal.
caption: (left) We extract patch representations from frozen, pre-trained ViTs and fit linear probes to predict figure-ground assignment on natural images, excluding patches that span both foreground and background (shown in black). We evaluate probes on both natural images and cue-controlled stimuli where textures are randomly replaced. (right) Probes for most models are largely unaffected by disrupting texture information, indicating the use of shape cues. Baselines rule out architectural biases and trivial strategies based on region area and location.
abstract: Rich perceptual structure emerges in modern vision encoders. Several studies have shown that the internal representation in many vision transformers separates foreground objects from the background, however, little is known about the visual cues that have been learned by these models. In this work, we study whether figure-ground organization in a broad range of 25 vision transformers relies on generalizable shape cues, rather than on superficial texture statistics. To do so we train linear probes to classify patches as figure or ground, and evaluate them zero-shot on synthetic stimuli where individual cues are systematically manipulated. For a broad range of vision encoders, we find that probes are robust to the random replacement of textures in the input image, suggesting that the emerging figure-ground organization relies on shape cues. Probes also generalize in a zero-shot fashion to synthetic images where individual shape cues, recognizability and spatial priors are controlled for. Our experiments reveal a strong influence of surroundedness and convexity cues, while results for parallelism and symmetry are more nuanced. More detailed analyses reveal stronger evidence for shape-based cues in larger models, that models trained for object-recognition tend to be less robust to texture changes and that figure-ground information emerges most prominently in middle layers. Taken together, our study demonstrates that emerging figure-ground organization in recent vision encoders relies strongly on generalizable shape cues, advancing our understanding of the internal processing in vision transformers, and opening an exciting avenue for computational research on human visual perception. Code and data is available at https://github.com/mtangemann/mlvbench.
